11531-the-life-of-marie-de-medicis-queen:
Julia Pardoe's first volume follows Marie de Medicis from her youth to her place as queen beside Henri IV of France, closing the opening book in 1599. It sets out Henri's earlier marriage to Marguerite de Valois, the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew, court plots, and Marguerite's return to France.

Court life, marriage bargains, and faction fill the chapters, with Catherine de Medicis pressing her daughter back toward Paris. Pardoe builds the life from chronicle and memoir, keeping the queen's rise, rather than her later regency, at the centre of this volume.
11600-the-life-of-marie-de-medicis-queen:
Julia Pardoe's second volume on Marie de Medicis, dated 1890, opens with book one, chapter nine, in 1610. Preparations for Marie's coronation at St. Denis, deferred and then resumed, fill the first pages, with a gorgeous procession and the anger of ex-Queen Marguerite.

The Comte and Comtesse de Soissons leave Paris, and Marie's court shines in full magnificence. Later chapters follow the regent's grief over a murdered adherent, M. de Luz, killed at a second pass after she had pardoned him. The volume carries Marie from queen consort into the hard years of regency.
11601-the-life-of-marie-de-medicis-queen:
Julia Pardoe's third volume on Marie de Medicis follows the queen-mother into exile, opening in 1618 with de Luynes resolved to keep her at Blois. Richelieu's treachery, Marie's suspicions, and her refused request to move to Monceaux set the tone.

A royal correspondence, court vanity, and a later meeting where Richelieu interrupts Marie closeted with the king carry the story forward. The volume closes the three-volume life begun in 1890, tracing a queen who had ruled as regent under Louis XIII into a life of plots, exile, and lost power.
8789-the-vision-of-hell-by-dante-alighie:
Dante Alighieri's Vision of Hell, illustrated by Gustave Dore and translated by the Reverend H. F. Cary, gives the complete Inferno in one volume, cantos one through thirty-four. Dante, midway through life, finds himself astray in a gloomy wood. Virgil leads him down through nine circles, from the unbaptized and the lustful to traitors frozen in ice at the centre. Dore's famous engravings, listed by canto in the original edition, match the poem's most terrible scenes.

Cary's translation, the first to make Dante widely known in English, keeps a dignified, early Victorian verse. The complete Inferno lets readers follow the whole descent without breaks, from the dark wood to Satan himself. It remains an ideal first Dante: a single, coherent passage through sin, punishment, and pity, with Dore's art as a visual companion to the poetry.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PetersPaulConra:
Russell Kent wrote 'What Did the Parkland Doctors Really Say?' for JFK Lancer, a research publisher. His subject is the doctors at Parkland Hospital who treated President Kennedy. Kent asks whether those doctors modified their descriptions of Kennedy's head injuries in later interviews.

The Parkland doctors' first accounts, given at a press conference that afternoon, described wounds in terms that later testimony seemed to soften. That difference has fueled argument for sixty years. Kent compares the early words with the later ones. His article is a study in how testimony drifts, and in why the first day's record matters to everyone who argues about the shooting.
the-life-of-marie-de-medicis-queen-of-fr: Julia Pardoe wrote her life of Marie de Medicis, consort of Henry IV and regent under Louis XIII, in three volumes issued in 1890. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here for volume one. Book one, on Marie as queen, opens with a chapter covering 1572 to 1599. Pardoe other court histories named on the page cover Louis XIV and Francis the First. The biography itself cannot be read in this record.
the-vision-of-hell-by-dante-alighieri-tr: Dante Alighieri's Vision of Hell, the Inferno, appears here in the English translation by the Reverend H. F. Cary, with illustrations by Gustave Doré. The pages present give the title and a list of cantos, so the poem itself does not appear. Thirty-four cantos are numbered in sequence, matching the full count of Dante's Hell. A heading for canto one follows the list, with no verse beneath it in what is preserved. Readers can identify the edition, its translator, and its illustrator from this record alone.
